Defintely recommend. If I could give it a score out of 10, I'd give it a 9.  The first chapter is a little slow, but when you get around half way through chapter two, it really starts to pick up.

The character building is genuine, and we all know a Harrison in real life :) The story is rich and choices really do matter. "Do I upload X or Y data? Do I upload it at all?!" Pretty much every piece of data you upload is referenced in some way, and major plot twists occur based on your decision to upload or not.

It took me 12 hours on my first playthrough because I read most things and accessed data multiple times to make sure my decisions were as accurate as I could make them.

The music is great. Never got tired of it.

Would highly recommend this game if you're in to story rich, choices matter, adventure games.

Wow, just wow! The concept is so original that I've never seen anything even remotely close. I guess I'm going back for another playthrough tomorrow.

Orwell is what I expected it to be. A deep, intriguing story, which pulls you in so deep that you begin to question your own actions afterwards. I sort of fell into this fever of giving Orwell any obtainable information without hesitation. It leaves me kind of shocked about myself.

It is also a warning, because Orwell isn't fantasy or far away from our every day lives. Dating apps, Facebook etc. they reveal everything about us, but in the end I think the true message of Orwell is the last conversation, which I'm not going to spoil.

I would love to have more campaigns within the same engine, just different settings or stories. Maybe with some Cameos from this one.

Ok Honestly this game is a treat. Incredibly interesting themes showing a modern interpretation of the prologue to 1984 in a sense. The mechanics work really well, making your decisions hold weight and using your own progress play into the games narrative hands (you'll see what I mean near the end). The music is well done too, a lovely little score playing in the background that never became annoying and felt at ease with the visuals and what I was doing, with some incredibly well timed swells in music and emotion as twists were revealed, something rather hard for a game which is mostly reading.
To explain what made me love the game is to describe a singular moment. Orwell floods you with information that seems useful and useless at the same time, using a highlighting system where certain phrases, words, numbers are made available to you to drag over to the left and thus profile your target. This occurs while reading throught the information, so it will pop up and if you are lazy, make you reliant on it, you may rush through the first couple hours just relying on this system, easy enough. But there was a point where I had to choose between two pieces of information to submit, and none of the lists of highlights I had collected seemed to help. Thankfully I like to take my time with my games and so had been reading everything carefully for intentions of characters and the like. Which made it all the more satisfying and magical when it clicked. When I realised that I had vague recollections of a small part of a post that I had read 30 minutes ago (I did say I like to take my time). This post had no highlights. The mechanics had not made me look at it. There was no cue on screen saying, "looking at this bit may help you decide on your answer". It was just me and my memory, rewarding me for actually paying attention to the game, I felt intelligent and attentive, even more so when it helped me make the correct choice without relying on luck.
I'm even going to replay it, something I've never done with an intensely story driven game like this, where I know how it unfolds. This will easily stay in my top ten for a long time I think.
There are only a couple of niggles I have on this game, one is that I kind of wish we had multiple cases to go through  instead of the large overarching one to see different uses and consequences to the use of Orwell, and the other is a technical one. At some point the game froze oddly and I had to quit out of the application, but thankfully the autosave is pretty damn sold and I never lost more than a few seconds of gameplay, I assume every action is autosaved and is the reason fo that.

I don't know how I came across the game, I had never heard of it until last week. I'm very familiar with George Orwell's 1984 so when I saw this game randomly I thought hell ya.

The gameplay is a bit like the old hacker's game "Uplink". Simple GUI that you, the "user" sit's behind a virtual system to do your work. 

Gameplay: It may seem like you have to do a lot of reading but this "Orwell" system tends to pick out what it thinks is important and relevant information. It's up to you to deem it important. If it is important, it'll unlock new stuff for you to read and so forth. At times you'll get conflicting information, this is the best part of the game as you have to decide, based on the profile you built on the person, which piece of information fits the puzzle.

You can read deeper into emails if you want, it makes you feel more part of the story and the world but you can also skim quite a bit, you'll just miss out on feeling like you know these people, without actually meeting them, it's a little creepy.

Story: It's great. At first I was a little detached from it because I didn't know if a game like this was going to be able to have a deep story. It does. It's told through emails, text messages, phone calls etc.

Took me 6 hours to complete and I don't feel a single one of those minutes was a waste.

The art style was great. I loved the polygon look while still being detailed.

Interface is super easy to use, they did a really good job on this.

Feels like "drag and drop everything from right to left" - thats your investigation. 
You have more "real choices" in a textadventure from the 80's.
Orwell is a very thought-provoking game with interesting decisions and choices, I highly recommend buying the game and playing it for yourself because it is an experience.

Those where entertaining 5 hours on my 1st playthrough.

The most intriguing part of the game is that the player as a person, not a a character, becomes part of the surveillance-machine with his actions and decisions. The Information you collect molds the picture of the person you investigate. You decide, which information get into the file and, if there are conflicting chunks (articles from different times, statements from different persons, rumors), which one will get into the system. Every chunk you pass is treated as a fact by the system and nactions on these are mandatory, so beware of consequences. It's terrifying how easy it is to put those people you check in categories and how the investigations progress while you play.

Regarding the presentation, the player sees what the character sees (i.e, the orwell-UI, apart from the intro), there's no speech and the art-style of the photos may not be everyone's taste and sometimes look strange. Nevertheless, the game still manages to evolve an intense atmosphere after the 1st episode with almost text only, only by viewing live-chat and call protocols.

All usable data-chunks are marked by orwell and only (more or less) relevant information for the current day are available. Even if you could add information for a person's file which WILL become relevant later, orwell wouldn't let you create a file on that person until the game tell you to. The player may encount "useful" information which is not a chunk and can not be added to the file. Although this is counter-intuitive sometimes, this mechanism keeps the game on track and the player only focuses on relevant events and persons. Just think: If you can not add it, it's not relevant to the plot or you can get the same information from elsewhere.


All in all, a good expierence and i was surprise on how the narrative and the mechanics both worked out.

What a fantastic experience. Orwell is a text-based game with a fairly linear progression. You play an investigator who uses an all-encompassing crowdsources surveillance system called Orwell. You are tasked with uncovering and identifying members of an alleged domestic terrorism group called "Thought" in the fictional country called "The Nation." You work your way through this task by investigating the phone calls, texts, emails, social media, dating profiles, bank information, and relationships of the various "suspects." You take snippets of highlighted information and upload them to Orwell (an irreversable process). It's up to you to decide, at times, which data is relevant. Choose poorly, and you can cause the deaths of certain suspects.

 If you hadn't guessed, this game is like an interactive modern version of the book "1984" by George Orwell (my favorite book of all time, by the way.) It offers a striking glimpse into what a complete surviallance state would look like in the modern world, and what the benfits and pitfuls to such a system may be. The game is pretty short at around 4 hours, but that's really all it needed to be. It definitely lacks replayability, but I don't think the story would have the impact of the first playthrough if I were to play it again. If you're interested in the subect matter or in story-based games in general, play Orwell. If you're looking for action or exploration, seek elsewhere. Just be mindful, because you never know who is watching.

It makes you feel righteous or deceitful, evil or good, and only when I beat the game did I look back and see that every piece of data I collected impacted the outcome. This was by far the best game I personally have played in a long time and five hours of my life that I will never want back. The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.

This game I would personally consider not only a game, but also a work of art. I believe the statement this game makes with the morality of governemnt involved in the lives of people over the internet is a must buy if you are willing to defend the Nation.
Fun Thriller. Decent Story. Lots of reading. You play as an internet detective, tasked with reading articles and communications in order to prevent tragedies.

Fantastic, thought provoking game. I didn't expect to enjoy a game this text-heavy as much as I did, but Orwell manages to make what is essentially a lot of reading very suspenseful and fun. This game tests your ability to discern fact from fiction and deal with extreme cognitive dissonance. It also offers a deep critique of the modern surveillance state by offering a succinct example of its negative implications. Whole things takes about 4-6 hours and merits multiple playthroughs.

This game is absolutely amazing. Without a doubt the most important game every made with a focus on personal liberties in a digital age. It addresses the complex issues of the ethics of digital surveilance and how a government can corrupt its self trying to do the right thing for the wrong reasons. If you have any interest in what the world would look like if the government could arbitrarily ingest your data and then put it in front of a third party to "interpret" then you WILL love this game.

Expect 4 hours of gameplay from this game, so decide on your own it if worth your money if not on discount.

The game is story-rich and the story is quite nice too. Requires a lot of reading, and I would say it is more a VN than a game, but I'd rather read VNs if they were presented in unique forms such as this game.

Great narrative! I felt very involved and a couple of times got intense chills when discovering various facts that completely altered my impressions. I wish I could say I got the same positive impression of the ending that everyone else did but I found myself confused about what to do to accomplish a couple of the endings. I felt that part was a bit odd. When I finally did end the game I hadn't meant to - I just didn't realise what I was doing would cause the game to end immediately. A bit sad because I think there was more for me to discover.

That doesn't change the fact that I overall loved this game, but I will also note that it was a bit short. I bought it as a part of a bundle on discount, so it was around 6 or 7 dollars. While technically there is replayability, you have to go back through a lot of content to get there. I might try again at some point, but not sure if I want to spend another four hours doing something I could just look up the results of on youtube.

Overall I recommend this game but I feel like it's really only worth it when on sale. I wish there was more content. I would love an extended sequel of some sort that followed multiple plots like this.

It's borderline but I'd lean towards no.

Effectively choose your own adventure, with the agency being 'what you leave out' by not reporting it to the agency.
The problem is some things are required to be reported to move the plot forward, and those aren't marked in any special way. Thus, there were a few times where I just started reporting everything, even if I wanted to leave it out.

Additionally, the plot anded up being "mass surveillance is bad" (obviously given the title), but by being "reports everything" robot, I caught two mass murderers, and wasted one innocent person's time in jail for a few days. Then I was lectured by a mass murderer and an anti-government hacker for 5 minutes, while waiting for the police to take the murderer away.

Somehow the terrible writing has pushed me more towards being pro surveillance lol.

Finally, it's really short (3hr), but I got it for 6 bucks, so I think I got my money's worth.

Overall like I said really borderline, but I wouldn't recommend it to most people.
